Title: Leveraging digital capabilities for supply chain recovery and renewal: the mediating roles of spontaneous and creative improvisation
Authors: Lei Wang, Chun Zhang
Affiliations: Glorious Sun School of Economics and Management, Donghua University; Grossman School of Business, University of Vermont
Abstract: Purpose Building on the dynamic capability view (DCV) and supply chain (SC) literature on digitalization, improvisation and resilience, we examined how different digital capabilities influence different post-disruption SC resilience outcomes (recovery and renewal) through distinct forms of improvisation in cross-border SCs. Design/methodology/approach Our sample comprises 217 matched Chinese supplier–buyer dyads, with buyers located in 66 countries. Confirmatory factor analysis and multiple regression were used to test the measurement model and hypothesized relationships, respectively. Robustness and endogeneity tests were also performed. Findings We find that digital market orientation is positively associated with creative improvisation, while its relationship with spontaneous improvisation is non-significant. In contrast, digital process innovation is positively associated with spontaneous improvisation, while its relationship with creative improvisation is non-significant. Furthermore, spontaneous improvisation is positively associated with SC recovery, while creative improvisation is positively associated with SC renewal. Creative improvisation mediates the relationship between digital market orientation and SC renewal, while spontaneous improvisation mediates the relationship between digital process innovation and SC recovery. Originality/value This study reveals distinct paths through which different digital capabilities contribute to post-disruption SC resilience. By differentiating digital capabilities, improvisational capabilities, and resilience outcomes, the study extends DCV-based SC resilience research by explaining how the adaptive potential embedded in these digital capabilities is translated through distinct improvisational capabilities into post-disruption SC resilience outcomes in cross-border SCs.
Journal: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

Title: Towards Maximum Throughput in Generalized Automated Transport Networks
Authors: Xiangdong Chen, Xi Lin, Fang He, Meng Li, Zuo-Jun Max Shen
Affiliations: Department of Civil Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China; and Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, National University of Singapore, 117576 Singapore; Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109; Department of Industrial Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China; Business School, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China
Abstract: Leveraging the connectivity and automation of vehicles to enhance traffic and logistic control is an important yet challenging topic in future city operations and industrial settings. One of the central questions is how to characterize and optimize the capacity of automated transport systems, a problem complicated by network topology, demand heterogeneity, and stochastic dynamics. Rhythmic control (RC) is a recently proposed scheme that integrates performance guarantees, generality, and conceptual simplicity, thereby enabling a tractable analysis of network-level capacity. This paper undertakes a rigorous theoretical investigation into the capacity of generalized automated transport networks, covering both one-way and two-way configurations. By abstracting infrastructures such as road networks, warehouse aisle systems, and port yard lanes into rhythmic networked systems, RC provides a unified analytical framework for evaluating throughput and stability across diverse automated transport domains. Within a static analytical setting, we formally characterize the notion of demand accommodation associated with a rhythm design. Under a stationary stochastic framework, we establish that RC achieves throughput optimality; however, accommodation alone does not guarantee stabilization under the same rhythm design, and stabilizing certain demand patterns may require excessively long cycle lengths. To mitigate this drawback, we introduce a variant of RC that incorporates strategic holdings. We demonstrate that, under mild conditions, this extension guarantees the stabilization of any accommodatable demand and achieves approximate throughput optimality under finite cycle lengths, with explicit throughput and stability guarantees that support refined rhythm design and capacity analysis. Extensive simulation studies are conducted to evaluate the performances of the proposed RC. The results verify its core effectiveness, demonstrate that a period-wise design enables adaptation to time-varying flows, and show that strategic holdings significantly enhance overall system efficiency. Title: Parental Response to Fetal Shocks and Macroeconomic Volatility
Authors: Rakesh Banerjee, Farhan Majid
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Exeter r.banerjee@exeter.ac.uk; mfarhanmajid@gmail.com
Abstract: Abstract We examine parental response to a fetal shock using data from 150 Demographic and Health Surveys in 50 developing countries. Focusing on the impact of Ramadan fasting, a common shock experienced by more than a billion Muslims worldwide, we find that children exposed to Ramadan fasting during pregnancy have lower rates of full vaccination for DPT and polio compared to their non-exposed siblings. Further, parents tend to compensate for the fetal shock during booms and reinforce during economic downturns. Our estimations suggest that this has resulted in approximately half a million excess infant deaths over the past three decades.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Hostility, Population Sorting, and Backwardness: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from the Red Army after WWII
Authors: Christian Ochsner
Affiliations: CERGE—EI Prague, CESifo, SIAW at the University of St. Gallen, and University of Lucerne. CERGE-EI—A joint workplace of Charles University and the Economics Institute of the Czech Academy of Sciences, Politickych veznu 7, 111 21 Prague, Czech Republic, Phone: +420 224 005 173 christian.ochsner@cerge-ei.cz
Abstract: Abstract How can short episodes of localized hostility shape regional economic trajectories that even amplify over time? I exploit economic differences across the idiosyncratic and short-lived line of contact between the Red Army and the Western Allies in South Austria at the end of WWII. The 74-day hostile presence of the Red Army shaped the age- and occupation-structure via refugee flows, causing amplifying demographic effects over time and backwardness in sector development and tax revenues. My findings also point to the isolated role of the Red Army’s hostile actions after WWII in understanding the European economic East-West divide.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Blended Finance and Female Entrepreneurship
Authors: Halil İbrahim Aydın, Çağatay Bircan, Ralph De Haas
Affiliations: CBRT Halil.Aydin@tcmb.gov.tr; Amazon and UCL bircanca@amazon.co.uk; EBRD, KU Leuven, and CEPR dehaasr@ebrd.com
Abstract: Abstract We study the real and allocative consequences of relaxing gender-specific credit constraints by analyzing a blended finance program designed to expand bank lending to female entrepreneurs in Turkey. Merging credit registry, tax, and matched employer-employee data, we find participating banks raised their credit share to women by over 18%, spanning repeat, poached, and first-time borrowers. Beneficiary firms invest more, grow employment, sales, and profits, diversify their networks, and exit less. Treated banks also expand lending to male entrepreneurs, though the increase is smaller and disproportionately directed toward higher-productivity firms, suggesting reallocation rather than crowding out. District-level effects are absent, reecting the program’s modest scale.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Tax Incentives and Return Migration
Authors: Jacopo Bassetto, Giuseppe Ippedico
Affiliations: University of Milan, IAB, RF Berlin; University of Nottingham, CESifo, IZA, RF Berlin
Abstract: Abstract We study how tax incentives affect the return migration of high-skilled expatriates to their home country, exploiting a generous income tax break for returnees in Italy. Using administrative data and a Triple-Difference design, we estimate a migration elasticity to the average net-of-tax rate just below one. Responses are sizable across the upper half of the earnings distribution, indicating that tax-induced migration is not limited to top earners. A cost-benefit analysis reveals that, while costly in the short term, the scheme pays for itself in present value if a sufficiently large fraction of returnees remains after the scheme elapses.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Is American Soft Power a Casualty of the Trade War? Evidence from U.S. Movie Viewership in China
Authors: Haichao Fan, Yichuan Hu, Lixin Tang, Shang-Jin Wei
Affiliations: School of Economics, Fudan University, Shanghai, China fan_haichao@fudan.edu.cn; School of Economics and Management, Tongji University, Shanghai, China huyichuan175@gmail.com; Institute for Economic and Social Research, Jinan University, Guangzhou, China lixintang@jnu.edu.cn; Columbia University, New York, New York, USA shangjin.wei@columbia.edu
Abstract: Abstract The US trade war against China can either enhance or diminish American soft power in China, depending on whether Chinese citizens view it as legitimate. We study how US movie viewership, a measure of American soft power, responds to the trade war. We find a significantly greater reduction in US movie viewership in regions more exposed to the Trump tariffs, but no corresponding decline in non-US movies. The decline is stronger for action and drama movies, which tend to embody greater perceived “Americanness.” Survey data also show a sharper decline in trust in Americans in more tariff-exposed regions.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Structuring Cash Transfers: Cash Flow Preferences, Seasonality, and Financial Decisions in Rural Kenya
Authors: Carolina Kansikas, Anandi Mani, Paul Niehaus
Affiliations: University of Cambridge; University of Oxford; UC San Diego
Abstract: Abstract We examine the preferences of low-income households in Kenya over the structure of unconditional cash transfers. Most preferred lumpy transfers, and some preferred deferred receipt—in contrast to the typical structures of safety-net programs, but consistent with evidence on the financial challenges of poverty. Turning to consequences, receiving transfers later in the year raised income 1.5 years later—but willingness to defer receipt was sensitive to small changes in cash flow around the time of decision-making. Taken together, these results illustrate how adapting cash transfer design to the decision-making environment of those in poverty could improve financial choices and outcomes.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: The Female Sensitivity Hypothesis: Evidence From Experimental Economics
Authors: Felipe A. Araujo, Neeraja Gupta, Lise Vesterlund
Affiliations: Lehigh University; University of Richmond; University of Pittsburgh and NBER
Abstract: Abstract We assess the empirical evidence for the hypothesis that women more than men respond to changes in treatment. First, we examine whether the results of over two hundred experimental economics papers support the female sensitivity hypothesis. Second, using data from two studies (DellaVigna and Pope, 2022; Exley et al., 2025), we conduct over two hundred pairwise tests of the hypothesis. Both analyses show that gender is not predictive of responsiveness to treatment. We further examine how the hypothesis has been disseminated in the literature and find that it is referenced predominantly by papers that support it.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: The Equilibrium Effect of Information in Consumer Credit Markets: Public Records and Credit Redistribution
Authors: Scott L. Fulford, Éva Nagypál
Affiliations: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Scott.Fulford@cfpb.gov
Abstract: Abstract Information is central to consumer credit, but little is known about its equilibrium effects. We study a 2017 natural experiment in which non-bankruptcy public records were purged from U.S. credit reports. The large information-removal differences across states allow us to identify equilibrium impacts. Available credit increased for consumers who lost negative information directly. Consistent with our model, available credit declined indirectly for consumers who did not lose the negative information because they could no longer distinguish themselves. The direct and indirect effects nearly canceled, so the net equilibrium effect after a year was nearly zero but with substantial redistribution.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Contracting Structures in Public Procurement: Evidence from Donor-Funded Electrification in Kenya
Authors: Catherine D. Wolfram, Edward Miguel, Eric Hsu, Susanna B. Berkouwer
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology and NBER; University of California, Berkeley and NBER; University of California, Berkeley; University of Pennsylvania and NBER
Abstract: Abstract We study how contracting and monitoring structures in public procurement affect large-scale infrastructure construction. Starting in 2016, Kenya’s public electric utility ran competitive auctions and then awarded and administered dozens of procurement contracts to connect millions to electricity. The causal analyses leverage natural and experimental variation and granular, independentlycollected construction quality data. Kenya Power contracts funded by the World Bank featured unbundled contract components known as ‘design-bid-build’ and enhanced monitoring compared to African Development Bank-funded contracts. Unbundling contracts delayed construction progress but improved quality. Randomized inspections improved quality without large delays. Bundled contracting with additional independent monitoring could improve outcomes.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: How Credible Are the Findings from Online Experiments?
Authors: Abel Brodeur, Nikolai Cook, Anthony Heyes, Lamis Kattan
Affiliations: University of Ottawa abrodeur@uottawa.ca; Wilfrid Laurier University ncook@wlu.ca; University of Birmingham a.g.heyes@bham.ac.uk; Georgetown University in Qatar lk811@georgetown.edu
Abstract: Abstract Online experiments have surged in popularity, but how credible are their published results? We examine the universe of hypotheses tested on Amazon Mechanical Turk and reported in leading journals between 2010 and 2021. We find evidence of widespread p-hacking, publication bias, and under-powered studies. The extent of the problems varies substantially across fields, with marketing particularly badly afflicted and little evidence of distortion in economics. We explore correlates of increased credibility and compare the online results to laboratory results from the same outlets, finding similar distortions in both, with bunching just above the significance threshold more pronounced on MTurk.
Journal: The Review of Economics and Statistics

Title: Professional Networks and the Labour Market Assimilation of Immigrants
Authors: Olof Åslund, Mattias Engdahl, Sébastien Willis
Affiliations: Uppsala University; Institute for Evaluation of Labour Market and Education Policy (IFAU); Uppsala Center for Labor Studies; Centre for Research and Analysis of Migration (CReAM); Rockwool Foundation Berlin
Abstract: Abstract We examine how professional networks shape immigrants’ job search and labour market assimilation. Analysing displaced workers in Sweden, we show that connections to firms through conationals are especially important for immigrants’ job finding. As networks expand to include more natives, the value of such connections rises towards that seen for displaced natives. Origin homophily also predicts whether a connection provides a referral—increasing earnings and lowering turnover—rather than vacancy information. Networks account for 20 per cent of the growth in immigrants’ re-employment over their first decade after arrival; immigrants’ networks are as productive as natives’ after fifteen years.

Title: Cognitive ability, risk preferences and errors
Authors: Michalis Drouvelis, Graeme Pearce
Affiliations: University of Birmingham; CESifo, Munich; University of St Andrews
Abstract: Abstract In this paper we examine the link between cognitive ability, risk preferences and the errors that people make. We build a unique dataset that contains almost 260,000 decisions made under risk in a variety of tasks by approximately 13,000 individuals, with each person having completed a test designed explicitly to measure their cognitive ability. Our analysis suggests that intelligence has (1) no impact on risk preferences and (2) a robust link to errors. Our results have implications for the development of theories that seek to explain the impact of cognitive ability on decision making.

Title: Inventory adjustment under global supply chain pressure: the moderating role of working capital structure
Authors: Rahul Pandey, Farooq Durrani
Affiliations: The University of Memphis Department of Supply Chain Management; University of Louisville Department of Finance
Abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to investigate how global supply chain pressure affects firms' inventory adjustment and how this relationship depends on their working capital structure, specifically supplier trade credit, customer credit exposure, and liquidity. Design/methodology/approach We draw on organizational information processing theory and real options theory to develop hypotheses about how global supply chain pressure and working capital structure shape firm inventory adjustment. The hypotheses are tested using a panel of 214,674 firm-quarter observations from 6,499 publicly listed US manufacturing firms over 1998–2025. We employ a shift–share panel design with firm and quarter fixed effects for the empirical analysis. Findings The results reveal that firms increase inventory as global supply chain pressure rises, but the average buffering response masks substantial heterogeneity in how firms manage supply uncertainty. Firms with higher supplier trade credit and customer credit exposure respond more strongly by increasing inventory. Liquidity has the opposite effect. It weakens the inventory response and, at high levels, reverses it, indicating a shift toward flexibility preservation. Liquidity further conditions the role of supplier trade credit and customer credit exposure, such that supplier financing matters most when liquidity is scarce, whereas customer credit exposure becomes more consequential when liquidity is abundant. Originality/value This study contributes to inventory management research by integrating the buffering and flexibility preservation perspectives on inventory under uncertain supply chain conditions. It shows that rising global supply chain pressure does not uniformly lead firms to build inventory buffers. Instead, the balance between buffering and flexibility preservation depends on the working capital structure that supports or constrains inventory commitment. The study also advances a liquidity-centered account of inventory adjustment by showing that liquidity changes both the inventory response to global supply chain pressure and the roles of supplier financing and customer credit exposure in supporting inventory buffers under strained supply conditions.
Journal: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

Title: Biased by sustainability? How cognitive biases shape procurement decisions under information equivocality
Authors: Chiara Vagnini, Mariolina Longo, Matteo Mura
Affiliations: University of Bologna Department of Management
Abstract: Purpose Climate change introduces new informational asymmetries across supply chains, increasing managers' need to process sustainability-related information in procurement decisions. Such information is equivocal, making its interpretation challenging and increasing decision-makers’ susceptibility to cognitive biases. Building on organizational information-processing theory and behavioral decision-making research, this study examines how cognitive biases shape procurement decisions involving sustainability information. Design/methodology/approach We developed hypotheses on cognitive biases emerging from three characteristics of sustainability information: structural properties (risky choice framing, attribute framing, numeracy and anchoring), inferential dynamics (halo effect) and social influences (herd effect). We tested these hypotheses through between-subject vignette-based experiments depicting individual, one-shot procurement decisions. The experiments were conducted in person with 475 participants, including managers and students. Findings We found that sustainability-oriented procurement decisions are vulnerable to cognitive biases. In particular, biases induced by the structural properties of information produced the strongest effects across both managers and students, followed by distortions emerging from inferential dynamics. In contrast, socially driven distortions emerged only among students, suggesting that professional experience mitigates reliance on peer behavior. Originality/value This study extends organizational information-processing theory-based sustainable supply chain management research by demonstrating that individual-level cognitive biases shape the interpretation of sustainability information. In doing so, we characterize the interpretation stage as being sensitive to information architecture, inferential reasoning and, under conditions of social influence, the professional experience of the decision-maker. Finally, we provide guidance for designing sustainability information and procurement decision processes that reduce susceptibility to cognitive biases.
Journal: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

Title: Multi‐Agent Contracting With Network Externalities
Authors: Yang Sun, Wei Zhao
Affiliations: School of Economics Southwestern University of Finance and Economics Chengdu China; School of Economics and Management Tsinghua University Beijing China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper analyzes how the structure of externalities‐encompassing both pure spillovers and interactive components‐reshapes the classic trade‐off between incentives and risk in multi‐agent contracts. The interplay of network effects and moral hazard generates congestion effects among agents with a common neighbor, which we decompose into a sum of weighted Katz‐Bonacich centralities. This tractable characterization enables clear comparative statics on the externality structure. We further apply the framework to examine how organization structures shape firm boundaries, and the design of Pigovian taxes to generate social security.

Title: Will markets provide humane jobs?
Authors: Arash Nekoei

Title: Spanning boundaries to boost network engagement along implementation processes of digital technologies: evidence from a multiple case study in hospitals
Authors: Vincent Peters, Bieke Henkens, Tom A. E. Aben, Melissa De Regge
Affiliations: Tilburg University Department of Information Systems and Operations Management; Ghent University Department of Marketing, Innovation and Organization; Eindhoven University of Technology Department of Industrial Engineering and Innovation Sciences; Warwick Business School, University of Warwick; University Hospital Ghent Strategic Policy Cell
Abstract: Purpose This study investigates how boundary spanners realise network engagement during the implementation of digital technologies in healthcare operations, focusing on how actors connect diverse stakeholder groups across organisational, functional and professional boundaries. Design/methodology/approach A multiple case study was conducted in two hospitals implementing comparable digital technologies with contrasting outcomes. Data were collected through archival documents and two rounds of semi-structured interviews. By means of inductive analysis, we identified boundary-spanning roles and their contribution to network engagement across organisational, functional and professional boundaries. Findings The findings show that boundary-spanning roles operate not in isolation, but as a constellation that jointly activate, embed and legitimise across diverse groups of actors. Through this constellation, actors cross organisational, functional and professional boundaries, thereby supporting the implementation of digital technologies in healthcare operations. Originality/value This study contributes to healthcare operations literature by moving beyond single-organisation adoption models and introducing a network-based perspective on technology implementation. It advances boundary-spanning theory by conceptualising how boundary-spanning roles enable engagement across multi-actor networks, addressing a gap at the intersection of digital technology, healthcare operations and implementation. Practical principles are provided to guide managers in defining, supporting and leveraging boundary-spanning roles during technology implementation in healthcare operations.
Journal: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

Title: The Immigration Surplus Revisited
Authors: Michael Amior, Alan Manning
Affiliations: King’s College London; Hebrew University of Jerusalem; Centre for Economic Performance; London School of Economics
Abstract: Abstract We extend the immigration surplus results of Borjas (1995). In a closed competitive constant-returns economy, we show that an influx of migrants (holding their skill mix fixed) must increase the total real income of natives, for any number of factor inputs, any pattern of substitutability or complementarity between them, and any number of intermediate or final goods – with larger gains if natives and migrants differ more in skill mix. If natives supply labour elastically across skill types, their welfare gains are diminished, even if they respond by moving to higher-paying jobs. We illustrate our results using a US calibration.

Title: Networks of Dissent: Social Leaders and Protest in an Autocracy
Authors: Johannes Buggle, Max Deter, Martin Lange
Affiliations: University of Innsbruck; Berlin School of Economics, University of Potsdam , CEPA; ZEW Mannheim
Abstract: Abstract This paper examines how network ties between local social leaders influenced the diffusion of mass protests in an autocracy. We focus on the Protestant Church and the Peaceful Revolution in East Germany. To quantify the role of leader networks in protest diffusion, we compile biographical records of over 1,600 Protestant pastors and construct network ties based on shared employment histories. Our findings reveal that network connections led to an increase in protest diffusion by 7.1 percentage points in a given week. Evidence from quasi-random connections, placebo networks, and an IV strategy supports a causal interpretation of these results.

Title: National Wage Contracts, Monopsony, and Welfare in a North-South Economy
Authors: Emanuele Ciani, Alberto Dalmazzo, Guido de Blasio
Affiliations: Bank of Italy; University of Siena Deptment of Economics & Statistics
Abstract: Abstract In countries characterized by significant geographical disparities in productivity, nationwide labour contracts may cause local unemployment by preventing the adjustments that would occur in a competitive labour market. Here we argue, however, that when there are mobility frictions and monopsony power, nationwide contracts may still be preferable to local contracts. Using a spatial general equilibrium model calibrated on the Italian North-South divide, we suggest that nationwide wage contracts may still lead to narrower regional welfare gaps if monopsony power is sufficiently strong in low-productivity areas.
Journal: Journal of the European Economic Association

Title: Dynamic Electric Vehicle Routing Problem with Stochastic Requests
Authors: Junyu Jiang, Jian Zhang, Jakob Puchinger
Affiliations: Department of Electronic Business, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou 510006 China; and EM Normandie Business School, Métis Lab, 92110 Clichy, France; EM Normandie Business School, Métis Lab, 92110 Clichy, France; and Université Paris-Saclay, CentraleSupélec, Laboratoire Génie Industriel, 91190 Gif-Sur-Yvette, France
Abstract: The dynamic electric vehicle routing problem (DEVRP) is a variant of the classical dynamic vehicle routing problem, where electric vehicles (EVs) are employed to provide on-demand logistics services. We investigate the DEVRP with stochastic requests and proactive charging decisions, where an EV must optimize its route and energy management to maximize the number of served requests while adhering to constraints on battery capacity and depot deadline. We formulate the DEVRP as a route-based Markov decision process (MDP) model and develop two complementary solution approaches: (1) a perfect-information rollout (PIR) policy based on stochastic lookahead and (2) a deep Q-learning (DQN) policy based on neural networks. Compared with conventional stochastic lookahead policies, such as rollout, the PIR policy improves the quality of reward-to-go estimation by better utilizing stochastic information, and we design two adjustable acceleration mechanisms to improve its balance between efficiency and accuracy. Although the PIR policy performs all computation online and adapts well to various scenarios, the DQN policy relies on offline training of neural networks to achieve faster online decision making. We also propose enhancement techniques to improve the performance of DQN. Through extensive numerical experiments, we demonstrate the advantages of the proposed policies in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency over multiple state-of-the-art approaches (such as value function approximation and rollout). Compared with the best-performing benchmark approaches, our proposed policies improve the decision quality by up to 5.3% while reducing the online computation time by more than half. Moreover, the merits of proactively and partially charging the EV in the DEVRP are investigated and validated. Robustness experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed policies when demand prediction is inaccurate. Title: Growing Pains: Inefficient Resource Allocation in Emerging Economies
Authors: Li Anpeng
Affiliations: Liaoning University Shenyang People's Republic of China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates how economic catch‐up shapes resource allocation in emerging economies. I develop a model that features firm‐specific technology adoption and costly adjustment of production factors. Rapid technological progress during catch‐up creates strong demand for reallocating resources from slow to fast adopters, amplifying the consequences of adjustment costs. The amplification fades as technological change gradually slows during convergence to a more advanced and efficient steady state. I evaluate the model using Chinese and German enterprise data and find that differences in development stage account for at least 40% of their labour allocative efficiency gap.

Title: Aggregate fluctuations from firm comovement
Authors: Nahyeon Bak, Daisoon Kim

Title: Investment irreversibility in a granular world
Authors: Tatsuro Senga, Iacopo Varotto

Title: Data Is Key: AUDI 'S Journey to Data‐Driven Business Models
Authors: Pepe Bellin, Norbert Homner, Erwin Fielt, Sebastian Gabriel, Martin Matzner
Affiliations: Friedrich‐Alexander‐Universität Erlangen‐Nürnberg Nürnberg Germany; Audi AG Ingolstadt Germany; School of Information Systems Queensland University of Technology Brisbane Queensland Australia
Abstract: ABSTRACT Car manufacturers excel in leveraging new digital technologies through vehicle design but face challenges in using the data these technologies provide for innovation. In this practitioner paper, we analyse and report on the process AUDI, a German original equipment manufacturer (OEM) of premium automobiles, went through in developing and managing data‐driven business models. A detailed description of the three phases of the carmaker's journey from creating to scaling to capturing identifies the automotive industry's urgent need to standardise data, prioritise customer integration and overcome difficulties in determining the price of data. For other (European) car manufacturers developing and managing data‐driven business models, we also derive five lessons learned from our case regarding AUDI's efforts to address issues when leveraging car‐related data and present an industry outlook with remaining challenges.

Title: Emerging Resistance in the Digital Transformation of Public Transport: Older Passengers With Dementia and Experiences of Ecobiographical Disruption
Authors: James Rupert Fletcher
Affiliations: Information, Decisions and Operations Division, School of Management University of Bath Bath UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT The digital transformation of public transport is prone to resistance. Among the discontents of such transformation, older people and those living with cognitive impairments are repeatedly identified. Stereotypes assuming their innate resistance to technological change are widespread, but research shows that older people with dementia can have rich digital lives. This paper reports findings from an ethnography of public transport digital transformation with older passengers living with dementia in Greater Manchester, UK. Combining interviews, photography, poetry, route maps and contextual statistics, four cases illustrate the emergence of resistance to digital displays, cashless exchange, e‐ticketing and live routing. They reveal subtle, nuanced and contextually contingent resistances that emerge from digital transformation disrupting passenger ecobiographies—the rootedness of their lives in longstanding ecosystems. Findings show that everyday resistance can be small, transient and relational, and should be taken seriously as an indicator of potential injustices. Future initiatives should meaningfully include older and disabled users throughout to increase alertness to ecobiographical disruption and emerging resistance.

Title: Modelling phased railway infrastructure upgrades deployment with a case study to ERTMS roll-out
Authors: Pedro José Correia Duarte, Lucas P. Veelenturf, Dennis Huisman
Abstract: Modernisation of railway infrastructure can lead to significant improvements in the efficiency of train services. However, the deployment of the modernisation requires huge financial investments and is carried out over decades. Consequently, infrastructure upgrade decisions must be strategically planned over time. In this paper, we introduce the Railway Infrastructure Upgrade Deployment Problem (RIUDP) in which we optimize phased deployment of infrastructure upgrades in a railway network so that societal benefits, measured by the reduction in the travel times of all passenger trains, are maximized. This requires to compute a timetable for each potential deployment plan of the upgrades. To compute this timetable, we assume that the structure of the timetable is given. We formulate the RIUDP as a Mixed Integer Linear Program and solve it to optimality. We compare optimised solutions with solutions that mimic rule of thumb decisions based solely on the theoretical cost effectiveness of infrastructure upgrades. A detailed case study on the roll-out of ERTMS on the main Dutch railway network reveals that severe gains can be achieved using optimized timetables instead of the rule of thumb decisions. Finally, we study the impact of specific practical considerations such as regional equity and connectivity constraints on the RIUDP.

Title: Does the United States spend enough on public schools? Evidence from a market-based efficiency test
Authors: Patrick J. Bayer, Peter Q. Blair, Kenneth Whaley
Abstract: While existing evidence shows that increased school spending improves student outcomes, it remains unclear whether current spending levels are efficient. Building on the classic public finance insight that local public-goods provision is efficient when a marginal, tax-financed increase leaves local house prices unchanged, we test whether school spending meets this benchmark. To implement this test, we assemble a 26-year national panel linking house prices, current public school expenditures, and property taxes, and exploit court-mandated school finance reforms to develop new instruments for local taxation. Combining these instruments with established instruments for current expenditures, we estimate the causal effect of tax-financed spending increases on house prices. Tax-financed increases in current expenditures raise house prices, implying that households value additional school spending more than it costs. These findings indicate that current U.S. public school spending falls below the efficient benchmark.

Title: How do firms respond to parental leave absences?
Authors: Anne Ardila Brenøe, Urša Krenk, Andreas Steinhauer, Josef Zweimüller
Abstract: How do firms adjust their labor demand when a female employee takes temporary leave after childbirth? Using Austrian administrative data, we compare firms with and without a birth event and exploit policy reforms that significantly altered leave durations. We find three main results. First, firms respond primarily through anticipatory hiring, while medium-run effects on total employment and the wage bill are small. Second, these adjustments differ sharply by gender: anticipatory replacement hiring is overwhelmingly female, but firms’ workforce composition shifts toward men in the medium run, driven by the shorter tenure of female new hires and higher retention of male incumbents. Third, while longer leave entitlements substantially extend actual leave absences, we do not find systematic differences in firms’ labor demand responses across leave regimes. Taken together, these findings show that firms accommodate parental leave mainly through anticipatory hiring and gendered changes in workforce composition, with limited medium-run changes in aggregate labor demand even when leave durations differ substantially.

Title: Issue Information
Old but Sold? Innovation Through Tradition Strategy for Export and the Role of Family Involvement
Authors: Ivan Miroshnychenko, Lorenzo Ardito, Paolo Capolupo, Antonio Messeni Petruzzelli
Affiliations: Paris School of Business Paris France; Department of Mechanics, Mathematics and Management Polytechnic University of Bari Bari Italy; Mount Royal University Calgary Alberta Canada; Department of Management and Economics Pegaso Telematic University Naples Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the notable body of research, the family firm (FF) internationalization literature has overlooked the role of innovation strategies in explaining FFs' export performance. We focus on the innovation through tradition (ITT) strategy—specifically, the degree to which a firm leverages its firm‐specific, mature (i.e., past) knowledge in the innovation search and recombination process. This strategy is particularly relevant for FFs as it can have ambivalent effects on export performance. On the one hand, it may ease the liability of foreignness; on the other, it could exacerbate it, creating tensions that firms must carefully navigate. Drawing from the socioemotional wealth perspective, we argue that FFs will be more prone to adopt an ITT strategy. However, the extent to which they will be able to reap the advantages or suffer the constraints of such a strategy for export depends on the particular type of family governance. Specifically, we contend that family managers will have a positive moderating effect on the relationship between the degree to which a firm leverages firm‐specific mature knowledge and export intensity thanks to their direct involvement and operational control over innovation activities. Conversely, family owners lacking this direct involvement will have a negative moderating effect on this relationship. Our analyses, based on a global longitudinal sample of 134 listed firms in the automotive and pharma/biotech industries observed from 2008 to 2020, support our hypotheses. Our results contribute to the nexus of the FF internationalization and FF innovation literature streams, the ITT research in FFs, and the broader internationalization literature.

Title: Connecting Socioemotional Wealth to Green Product Innovation: The Role of Absorptive Capacity
Authors: Jonathan Bauweraerts, Unai Arzubiaga, Vanessa Diaz‐Moriana
Affiliations: Department of Control, Audit, Risk Management and Entrepreneurship University of Mons Mons Belgium; Department of Financial Economic I University of the Basque Country, UPV/EHU Bilbao Spain; Department of Business Organization and Marketing University Pablo de Olavide Sevilla Spain
Abstract: ABSTRACT Academic Summary As one of the main drivers of sustainable development, green product innovation (GPI) has received increasing attention from academia. However, few works have investigated this issue in the family business context, none of which directly address the role of family owners' nonfinancial preferences on GPI. To extend our knowledge on this topic, this study builds on the socioemotional wealth (SEW) perspective to investigate how SEW affects GPI in family firms, while also considering the mediating role of absorptive capacity. Drawing on the FIBER conceptualization of SEW, we relate five SEW dimensions to potential/realized absorptive capacity and GPI. Our empirical analysis on a sample of 249 private family firms indicates that family firms' inclination toward GPI depends on the SEW dimensions that are valued by the owning family. Furthermore, potential and realized absorptive capacity mediate the relationship between four SEW dimensions (family control and influence, identification of family members, binding social ties, and renewal of family bonds) and GPI. Overall, this study demonstrates the importance of considering the interrelation between family and organizational factors to understand green product innovation heterogeneity in the family business context. Managerial Summary This study explores how family owners' SEW preferences influence GPI through absorptive capacity. Our findings reveal that when family firms emphasize reputation, stakeholder trust, or continuity across generations, developing both potential and realized absorptive capacity is essential for driving GPI. To achieve this, we recommend that firms invest in cross‐functional collaboration, form partnerships with universities or research institutions, and implement training programs that keep employees informed about emerging trends and technologies. These practices strengthen the firm's ability to identify, integrate, and apply external knowledge, translating it into effective green product innovation strategies. Additionally, we find that when family firms prioritize control, GPI practices must adapt to preserve family decision‐making authority. Family‐led innovation teams and collaboration with trusted external advisors can help firms absorb external knowledge while safeguarding family influence. Therefore, we advise family businesses to tailor their knowledge management and innovation strategies to their specific SEW priorities in order to foster GPI. For policymakers, these findings highlight concrete pathways to support family firms' roles in green innovation, contributing to broader policy initiatives such as the European Union's research and innovation agenda.

Title: A Betrayal in the Family: An Inhibitor or Stimulus for Business Model Innovation?
Authors: Md Imtiaz Mostafiz, Nazha Gali, Farhad Uddin Ahmed, Mathew Hughes
Affiliations: University of Leicester School of Business, University of Leicester Leicester UK; Miyan Research Institute, IUBAT—International University of Business Agriculture and Technology Dhaka Bangladesh; University of Windsor Windsor Canada; Maynooth University Maynooth Ireland; University of Leicester Leicester UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT Academic Summary Business‐focused betrayals perpetrated by family members in managerial and decision‐making positions can devastate family businesses, questioning their assumptions about trust and how they conduct the business. Such betrayals ignite tensions between family and business logics, potentially causing paralysis and protection of the status quo or compelling innovation of its strategies and operations—its business model. We draw on two contrasting perspectives to examine this tension: the threat rigidity thesis suggests that betrayal inhibits business model innovation by inducing fear of failure (an emotional familial response); organizational learning theory suggests that betrayal stimulates business model innovation by prompting knowledge development (an impassive business response). Relying on a sample of family businesses from India ( n = 221) and Bangladesh ( n = 289), our results support the latter perspective. Our study provides a theoretical foundation for the relationship between business‐focused betrayal and business model innovation, revealing new mediating mechanisms and new insights into when and why the coupling of family and business logic prompts or impedes change. Managerial Summary Betrayal within family businesses resulting from the actions of family members in leadership or decision‐making positions can strike at the heart of trust and stability. Such moments often provoke powerful emotional reactions that lead to defensiveness, strained relationships, and resistance to change. Yet our findings reveal a more complex reality: betrayal can become a powerful catalyst for business model innovation. Rather than inherently damaging the family business, betrayal can disrupt entrenched routines, compel family business leaders to reassess priorities, and push family firms to explore new strategies, new practices, and innovative business models. The key to this innovation lies in reframing betrayal not as a threat, but as an opening for organizational learning, innovation, and growth. By acknowledging this dual nature, family firms can transform betrayal‐induced adversity into momentum. Doing so enables them to navigate emotional familial responses with impassive business responses that drive innovation to restore the strength, resilience, and competitiveness of the family business in time.

Title: Bridging Sustainability and Innovation in Family Firms: The Roles of Local Green Knowledge and Local Embeddedness
Authors: Josip Kotlar, Fernando Muñoz‐Bullón, Maria J. Sanchez‐Bueno
Affiliations: Department of Management, Economics and Industrial Engineering Politecnico di Milano Milano Italy; Universidad Carlos III de Madrid Department of Business Administration Getafe (Madrid) Spain
Abstract: ABSTRACT This article explores how family firms leverage environmental investments to drive innovation, proposing that their environmental efforts are more conducive to innovation compared to non‐family firms. We also propose that family firms' ability to transform environmental investments into superior innovation performance is particularly pronounced when they have easier access to local external green knowledge and when they are more locally embedded. Analysis of 1698 companies over the 2009–2017 confirms our hypotheses. The results bridge two key research streams—family firms' sustainability and innovation—that have remained largely disconnected so far, highlighting the role of environmental strategies as a crucial factor in explaining whether and under which circumstances family firms become more innovative than non‐family firms.

Title: Innovation in Family Firms: The Role of Absorptive Capacity and Knowledge Collaboration
Authors: David Bruce Audretsch, Maksim Belitski, Christina Guenther, Natalia Vershinina
Affiliations: Indiana University Bloomington Bloomington USA; Alpen‐Adria‐University Klagenfurt Klagenfurt Austria; Henley Business School University of Reading Reading UK; WHU‐Otto Beisheim School of Management Vallendar Germany; Audencia Business School Nantes France; IAE Paris ‐ Sorbonne Business School Paris France; Jönköping International Business School Jönköping University Jönköping Sweden
Abstract: ABSTRACT While prior research suggests that family ownership can significantly facilitate sales and innovation, empirical findings often overlook the nuanced differences in innovation inputs between family and non‐family firms. We address this gap by examining the extent to which family firms are able to use absorptive capacity by creating knowledge internally and collaborating with external partners to enhance their innovation. Utilizing micro‐level data from 9266 of the most innovative UK firms from 2006 to 2016, we employ a multi‐level analysis to examine how different knowledge inputs—such as internal investments in knowledge and external collaborations at the regional and international levels—influence innovation outputs in family and non‐family firms. Our findings contribute to the innovation and family business literature by providing a clearer understanding of the innovation dynamics within family firms compared to their non‐family counterparts. Additionally, we offer managerial insights and outline policy implications that could foster knowledge transfer in family firms. These recommendations take into account that regional and international knowledge collaboration serves as a boundary condition for family firms to outperform their non‐family counterparts.

Title: Keep Family Business Innovating: Revisit the Relationship Between Succession and Innovation From Ownership Succession
Authors: Yuan Chen, Weize Huang, Hanqing Chevy Fang, Ling Chen
Affiliations: School of Economics Zhejiang University Hangzhou China; Entrepreneurship and Enterprise Hub Xi'an Jiaotong‐Liverpool University Suzhou China; Department of Business and Information Technology Missouri University of Science and Technology Rolla Missouri USA; School of Management Zhejiang University Hangzhou China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how family owner‐manager successors' ownership influences R&D investment in family businesses. Drawing on the socioemotional wealth (SEW) perspective, we theorize that successors with higher family ownership prioritize extended SEW, leading to stronger R&D investment, while those with lower family ownership prioritize restricted SEW, resulting in weaker R&D investment. Additionally, we explore how family dynamics—specifically, the number of family directors and asymmetric salary favoring family members—moderate this relationship. Our findings enhance the understanding of successor heterogeneity and its impact on innovation, offering insights for succession planning that support the long‐term sustainability of family businesses.

Title: Women Directors and R&D Investment in Family Firms: The Mediating Role of Debt Financing
Authors: Francesco Paolone, Francesco Debellis, Hussain Muhammad, Stefania Migliori
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Statistics and Business Mercatorum University Rome Italy; Department of Marketing and International Business University of Vienna Vienna Austria; Department of Accounting and Finance American University of Ras Al Khaimah Ras Al‐Khaimah UAE; Department of Management and Business Administration University of Chieti‐Pescara Pescara Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT Although research examining the role of women directors in fostering innovation within family firms continues to expand, the mechanisms underlying their influence remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the mediating role of debt financing in the relationship between women directors and R&D investment. Drawing on upper echelons theory and the socioemotional wealth perspective, we theorize that women directors' heightened risk aversion and long‐term orientation lead family firms to adopt more conservative debt policies, thereby reducing financial constraints that typically discourage innovation. Using a longitudinal dataset of Italian listed family firms, we find that a greater proportion of women directors on the board is associated with lower levels of indebtedness, which in turn fosters increased investment in R&D. By identifying debt financing as a critical mechanism linking board composition to innovation strategy, this study advances theoretical understanding of how women directors influence innovation within family firms.

Title: In the Pursuit of Innovation: The Role of Top Management Team Functional Diversity and Open Discussion in Family Firm Innovation Intentions
Authors: Marco Mismetti, Paola Rovelli, Cristina Bettinelli, Mara Bergamaschi
Affiliations: Stockholm School of Economics, House of Innovation Stockholm Sweden; Faculty of Economics and Management Free University of Bozen‐Bolzano Bozen‐Bolzano Italy; Department of Management University of Bergamo Bergamo Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT Academic Summary Interest in family firm innovation has increased in recent times, generating the assumption that family firms are less willing to innovate than nonfamily firms. We investigate firm innovation inputs by examining whether family firms differ from nonfamily counterparts regarding innovation intentions. We then adopt an upper echelons perspective to study whether the TMT functional diversity and open discussion explain the alleged lower intention to innovate of family firms. The analysis of survey data from 393 Italian firms reveals that family firms are less willing to innovate than nonfamily firms and that the TMT functional diversity partially mediates this result, meaning that family firms develop lower innovation intentions due to their lower TMT functional diversity compared to nonfamily firms. Focusing on family firms, we find that the relationship between TMT functional diversity and innovation intentions is positively moderated by TMT open discussion. Our study shows that TMT functional diversity and TMT open discussion are essential to stimulate family firms' innovation intention, contributing to the family business innovation literature, the debate on the ability‐willingness paradox, and upper echelons research. Moreover, it provides practical implications by highlighting the importance of creating a functionally diverse TMT, while fostering open discussion among its members. Managerial Summary Our study highlights how family firms can overcome their lower intention to innovate compared to nonfamily firms. The analysis of survey data from 393 Italian firms highlights two key factors that help explain and address this gap: the functional diversity of the TMT and the presence of open discussion within the team. Our findings indicate that, because of their lower TMT functional diversity, family firms develop fewer intentions to innovate. Thus, family firms should invest at least as much as their nonfamily counterparts in TMT functional diversity. A practical way to do so is by promoting TMT appointment criteria to deliberately include individuals with varied functional backgrounds. However, diversity alone is not enough. An environment where TMT members feel encouraged to share doubts, opinions, and suggestions is essential to ensure that diverse knowledge is shared and used effectively. Together, these practices can significantly strengthen a family firm's intention to innovate. What is interesting about the implications of this study is that functional diversity and open discussion are not fixed traits; rather, they are strategic levers that leaders can shape over time to strategically refine and improve the attitudes toward innovation of their TMT and unlock their firm's innovation potential.

Title: Between Financial and Socioemotional Wealth: Navigating Knotted Tensions in Family Business Innovation
Authors: Elias Hadjielias, Michael Christofi, Carlotta Benedetti
Affiliations: Department of Management, Entrepreneurship and Digital Business Cyprus University of Technology Limassol Cyprus; Faculty of Economics and Business, Padjadjaran University Bandung Indonesia; Faculty of Economics and Business Administration, Vilnius University Vilnius Lithuania; Department of Management and Marketing University of Innsbruck Innsbruck Austria
Abstract: ABSTRACT Current research on family business innovation tends to isolate individual tensions for analysis, while in reality, these tensions often arise in complex entanglements. To fill this research void, we focus on understanding how multiple tensions occur in the innovation process, how these tensions are entangled, and how they are managed. We turn to the financial wealth–socioemotional wealth [FW‐SEW] trade‐off, which is a useful lens for understanding how family managers address tensions in a family business. We draw on a semi‐grounded multiple case study research that includes 51 in‐depth interviews across six private Cypriot family businesses. To assist in interpretation and analysis and enhance the robustness of our findings, we triangulate our data with 53 observations and 288 documents across the cases. We identify three knotted innovation tensions sensed by family managers based on the FW‐SEW trade‐off: inclusive innovation, stewardship‐focused innovation, and family routine innovation tensions. Our findings also reveal three corresponding strategies for managing knotted innovation tensions—controlled inclusivity, family‐driven responsible innovation, and fostering family‐business harmony—each aimed at balancing FW and SEW priorities. Our study re‐conceptualizes innovation tension management in the family business as entanglements of multiple tensions that must be properly sensed and managed.

Title: Leading by example: how major customers shape suppliers' implementation of process-based rights
Authors: Yinyin Cao, Yoon Hee Kim
Affiliations: College of Business, University of Michigan-Dearborn Department of Management and Marketing; Coles College of Business, Kennesaw State University
Abstract: Purpose Drawing from research on dependence and embeddedness in supplier-major customer relationships, this study examines the implementation level of process-based rights (PBR) – including freedom of association, workforce diversity, and fair and non-discriminatory treatment of workers – within supplier-major customer dyads. The study also empirically investigates how customers' transactional governance and relationship history with suppliers interplay in suppliers' PBR implementation. Design/methodology/approach Using 482 unique supplier-major customer dyads over 14 years (2010–2024), we performed hierarchical analysis to estimate the direct and interaction effects of customers' PBR implementation, transactional governance, and relationship history on their suppliers' PBR implementation. Findings Our results show that major customers exert a significant influence on suppliers' PBR implementation. Furthermore, transactional governance and a long relationship history work in synergistic ways only when the customer itself demonstrates average to high levels of PBR, but not when customer PBR implementation levels are low. Originality/value As one of the first studies to explore PBR within supplier-major customer dyads, our findings underscore the important role of customers in leading the implementation of labor standards, rather than as an enforcer of labor standards, in motivating supplier compliance.
Journal: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

Title: Immigration and the Slope of the Labour Demand Curve: The Role of Firm Heterogeneity in a Model of Regional Labour Markets
Authors: Andrea Ariu, Tobias Müuller, Tuan Nguyen
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Management and Quantitative Methods, University of Milan; CEPR, LdA, CESifo and CRENOS; University of Geneva; Institute of Economics and Econometrics, GSEM, University of Geneva
Abstract: Abstract In this paper, we provide new explanations for the puzzling findings that migrants do not decrease natives’ wages and that skilled immigration can increase them. We develop a model with regional labour markets and heterogeneous firms in which workers of different skill levels are imperfect substitutes, but for a given skill level, natives and migrants are perfect substitutes within a firm. In this setting, a skilled labour supply shock due to immigration induces skill-intensive firms to expand. These across-firm reallocations reduce the within-firm substitution between skilled and unskilled workers, thus limiting relative wage adjustments. When this mechanism is coupled with human capital externalities that are skill-neutral at the firm level but skill-biased on aggregate, the same skilled immigration shock can increase absolute and relative skilled wages. These two mechanisms are quantitatively important: the negative impact of immigration on natives’ wages is reduced by at least one-third when the across-firm reallocation mechanism is at work, and human-capital externalities can revert the sign of this relation.

Title: An exact solution algorithm for the bi-level optimization problem of electric vehicles charging station placement
Authors: Mobina Nankali, Michael W. Levin
Abstract: This work addresses electric vehicle (EV) charging station placement through a bi-level optimization model, where the upper-level planner maximizes charging revenue by selecting station locations under budget constraints, while EV users at the lower level choose routes and charging stations to minimize travel and charging costs. To account for battery range limitation, we construct a battery-expanded network and apply a shortest path algorithm with Frank-Wolfe traffic assignment. Our primary contribution is developing the first global solution algorithm for large scale EV charging station placement problems. We propose a Branch-and-Price-and-Cut algorithm enhanced with value function cuts and column generation. Our exact algorithm delivers solutions provably within the reported optimality gap of the global optimum with mathematical certainty. Computational experiments on the Eastern Massachusetts network (74 nodes, 248 links), the Anaheim network (416 nodes, 914 links), and the Barcelona network (110 zones, 1020 nodes, and 2512 links) demonstrate exceptional performance. Our algorithm terminates in a reasonable runtime while achieving optimality gaps below 1% across all instances. Controlled benchmarks against two genetic algorithms on identical instances confirm that the proposed algorithm finds equal or better solutions in less computation time across all tested networks. The algorithm successfully handles problems with over 300,000 feasible combinations, transforming EV charging infrastructure planning into a tractable optimization suitable for practical decision making on real-world networks with optimality guaranteed.

Title: Transit-MP: Transit-prioritized max-pressure control in sparse connected vehicle environments
Authors: Chaopeng Tan, Hao Liu, Dingshan Sun, Marco Rinaldi, Hans van Lint
Abstract: Max-pressure (MP) control stands out among real-time network traffic signal control methods due to its simplicity, decentralized nature, and theoretical stability. However, existing MP control methods have limited consideration of public transportation and do not address the network stability problem of transit-prioritized MP in partially connected vehicle (CV) environments. In this study, we propose Transit-MP, which realizes transit-prioritized MP control in partially CV environments by considering real-time vehicle occupancy and the impact of transit dwell at stations. Theoretically, we demonstrate that Transit-MP, while using different traffic state measures for upstream and downstream links for pressure calculation, still achieves road network stability even in partially CV environments. Note that for MP controllers in sparse CV environments, some movements may have missing CV observations, leading to link spillovers, which create the queue starvation phenomenon: a movement no longer receives the green phase despite the queue spillover. Therefore, we further propose a modified Transit-MP (mTransit-MP) that incorporates historical traffic data to address this issue. We rigorously prove that the proposed mTransit-MP can effectively avoid the queue starvation phenomenon. Experimental results on a real-world corridor in Amsterdam with 15 transit lines and 31 stations show that our method significantly reduces the real-time vehicle and spillover count, and improves delays for both private vehicles and transit vehicles compared to a state-of-the-art MP controller for transit signal priority. In sparse CV environments, our mTransit-MP is effective in mitigating link spillovers while enhancing the overall performance of multi-modal traffic.

Title: Structural transformation towards healthcare
Authors: Fil Babalievsky

Title: The welfare effects of explicit and implicit subsidies on fossil fuels
Authors: Tim Kalmey, Sebastian Rausch, Jan Schneider

Title: Digital tokens reshape ownership, control, and labor: organizing logics in DAOs
Authors: Nina-Birte Schirrmacher, Michel Avital, Johannes Rude Jensen, Omri Ross
Affiliations: The University of Sydney; Copenhagen Business School; University of Copenhagen

Title: Conflict or Compromise? Theory and Evidence from Africa and Asia
Authors: Rogerio Santarrosa
Affiliations: Insper Institute of Education and Research
Abstract: Abstract Civil wars are a recurring phenomenon undermining development in weak states. Faced with the possibility of costly conflict, why don’t leaders share power? I investigate the role of an unexplored commitment problem, both theoretically and empirically. The model features a leader who can appease challengers by sharing power, but doing so increases their effectiveness at launching a rebellion. I show that commitment worsens as the opposition becomes stronger, and derive testable non-monotonic implications of group strength on power-sharing and conflict. As challengers become stronger, the likelihood of inclusion (positive transfers) increases up to a threshold, beyond which the leader prefers to exclude an opposing group and face conflict. I test the model using data on politically relevant ethnic groups in Africa and Asia, their access to executive power, and on armed organizations that claim to represent them. I use within-country variation in population share to proxy for group strength. The empirical findings strongly accord with the predictions of the theory. I then structurally estimate the model parameters and explore policy-relevant counterfactuals, including the effects of democratization, changes in military capacity, financial aid, sanctions, and quotas.
Journal: Journal of the European Economic Association

Title: The Dynamics of the Racial Wealth Gap
Authors: Dionissi Aliprantis, Daniel R. Carroll, Eric R. Young
Affiliations: ENS de Lyon Lyon France; Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland Cleveland Ohio USA; University of Virginia Charlottesville Virginia USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study the dynamics of the racial wealth gap (the wealth of Black households relative to white ones) using a dynamic equilibrium model of overlapping generations. We match the model to the cross‐sectional distributions of wealth and earnings by race. We find that equalizing earnings is critical for permanent reductions in racial wealth inequality, and that one‐time transfers will have only transitory effects unless earnings are also equalized. Our results are robust to the introduction of racial differences in returns to saving, which only matter after earnings inequality is reduced.

Title: Debt Aversion: Theory and Measurement
Authors: David Albrecht, Thomas Meissner
Affiliations: WZB Berlin Social Science Center Berlin Germany; Maastricht University Maastricht the Netherlands
Abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a model of debt aversion and conduct an experiment with real debt and saving contracts to jointly elicit debt aversion and preferences over time, risk, and intertemporal losses. We find that 89% of participants are debt averse, which strongly influences their choices. The estimated “borrowing premium,” the compensation an average person requires to accept debt, is around 16% of the principal. Applying a validated survey module to a representative sample of German households, we find that debt aversion is both statistically and economically significantly associated with actual debt‐taking and financial health.

Title: Inter-organisational Capabilities and the Transformation of Trust in Blockchain-based Smart Contracts: A Framework for SME Ecosystems
Authors: Maksym Koghut, Cathy Urquhart, Soo Hee Lee, Omar Al-Tabbaa
Affiliations: University of Kent; Manchester Metropolitan University - All Saints Campus; University of Leeds
Abstract: Blockchain-based smart contracts embed agreement enforcement within executable code, constraining the partner discretion that inter-organisational relationships (IORs) have traditionally coordinated through trust, communication, and relational governance. This raises a question that popular accounts tend to foreclose: whether automated enforcement makes inter-organisational trust unnecessary, or whether trust instead changes in function and object. Drawing on expert consultation with 28 blockchain specialists and 25 in-depth interviews with executives, we conduct an inductive study of how IORs transform as organisations adopt smart contracts. We develop a framework in which intensive relational exchange enables organisations to build two inter-organisational capabilities, Distributed Transparency Capability and Algorithmic Coordination Capability, through which they actualise the affordances that smart contracts offer. Through this capability development a distinctive inter-organisational trust form emerges, System-based Trust, defined as warranted reliance on coordinating infrastructure that partner organisations jointly construct. System-based Trust complements rather than replaces relational trust: it carries operational coordination and frees relational trust for strategic collaboration and exception handling, producing Hybrid Inter-organisational Relationships as the outcome of successful transformation. The framework applies to small and medium-sized enterprise ecosystems with limited numbers of trading partners; larger-scale consortia and power-asymmetric networks fall outside its scope. Our findings reposition smart contracts as occasions for capability development rather than substitutes for inter-organisational trust.

Title: Operations optimization in multi-modal relay-based delivery systems: Plan-based model and nested exact algorithm
Authors: Xueting He, Lu Zhen, Shuaian Wang, Gilbert Laporte
Abstract: This study investigates the operational optimization of an on-demand, multi-modal relay-based delivery system comprising dispersed unmanned hub stations and fleets of drones and unmanned vehicles. We formulate a plan-based model to coordinate and synchronize heterogeneous delivery modes, ensuring timely and cost-effective fulfillment of customer orders. The proposed model determines which orders to accept in each arriving batch, allocates drones and vehicles to execute these orders, and schedules their movements to guarantee on-time deliveries. A nested exact algorithm, integrating logic-based Benders decomposition (LBBD), column-and-row generation (CRG), and branch-and-price (BP), efficiently solves typical instances in approximately 70 seconds. The algorithmic novelty lies in that a CRG & BP based exact algorithm is embedded in an LBBD to solve the LBBD's subproblem. Computational experiments, based on realistic scenarios, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methodology and provide several managerial insights. Factors such as average delivery distance, time-window flexibility, and fleet composition are shown to significantly impact system profitability and service quality. The results offer practical guidance on batch sizing, fleet configuration, and operational conditions under which multi-modal relay-based delivery systems outperform traditional courier-based models.

Title: Editorial Board
Trade, Human Capital, and Income Risk
Authors: Liuchun Deng, Pravin Krishna, Mine Z Senses, Jens Stegmaier
Affiliations: Duke Kunshan University, China and Halle Institute for Economic Research; Johns Hopkins University; Institute for Employment Research
Abstract: Abstract In this paper, we study the causal relationship between trade exposure and individual income risk, with emphasis on the role of human capital. We use a rich worker-level longitudinal dataset from Germany spanning the period 1976-2012, and find industry trade exposure to be causally related to income risk: Imports increase risk and exports decrease risk in an economically significant manner. Importantly, there is a complex interplay between human capital and the linkage between trade and risk: On average, individuals with higher levels of industry- or occupation-specific human capital experience lower risk. However, an increase in industry net imports increases risk more for workers with higher levels of industry tenure. Although net imports are also associated with declines in the mean income of these workers, the estimated effect on income levels is economically small. Our welfare framework, which jointly considers both mean income and income risk, shows that the welfare consequences of trade exposure are quantitatively dominated by the risk channel.
Journal: Journal of the European Economic Association

Title: Modeling and simulating human behavior in large-scale emergency evacuations: A comprehensive review
Authors: Shiva Moslemi, Ada Arıkanoğlu, Vedat Bayram, Barış Yıldız
Abstract: Disasters pose persistent threats to human life and infrastructure, making evacuation planning vital for disaster risk reduction. The effectiveness of such efforts depends on understanding and accurately modeling human behavior. This study reviews 479 peer-reviewed articles on large-scale evacuation planning and management, classifying them along two dimensions: behavioral factors influencing key authority-issued decisions and modeling approaches incorporating these dynamics within optimization, simulation, and simulation–optimization frameworks. While demographic and route-choice behaviors are extensively studied, mode selection and road-segment designation remain largely unexplored. Optimization models commonly assume full- or non-compliance, with limited research that considers partial-compliance, leading to more realistic solutions. On the other hand, simulation-based studies capture dynamic and uncertain conditions more effectively but are dominated by rule-based behavioral proxies, particularly for departure timing and route choice, and typically limit dynamic feedback to route choice alone. Simulation–optimization approaches, while increasingly adopted, remain largely reliant on parameter-based behavioral representations rather than empirically calibrated, behavior-oriented coupling. Emphasizing the importance of embedding behavioral heterogeneity in model structures, this review develops a taxonomy, highlights research gaps, and outlines future directions for behaviorally realistic evacuation models that enhance the effectiveness and practicality of evacuation strategies in real-world crises.

Title: Correction
Investment-goods market power and capital accumulation
Authors: Fabio Bertolotti, Andrea Lanteri, Alessandro T. Villa

Title: Information design in repeated interaction
Authors: João Correia-da-Silva, Takuro Yamashita
Abstract: How does a long-term relationship affect communication among economic entities? In this paper, we study dynamic information design in a simple “agreement game” with repeated interaction, where the state is imperfectly persistent. Disclosing information now influences future belief evolution, which results in a novel distortion relative to the static counterpart. We observe that the interaction of the players’ patience and the state’s persistence parameters is crucial in determining the optimal mechanism. Though an efficient mechanism is optimal with sufficiently small or large patience, with intermediate levels of patience, optimal mechanisms exhibit excessive agreement when states are sufficiently persistent, while they exhibit excessive disagreement with less persistence. How does a long-term relationship affect communication among economic entities? In this paper, we study dynamic information design in a simple “agreement game” with repeated interaction, where the state is imperfectly persistent. Disclosing information now influences future belief evolution, which results in a novel distortion relative to the static counterpart. We observe that the interaction of the players’ patience and the state’s persistence parameters is crucial in determining the optimal mechanism, where both excessive agreement and excessive disagreement can arise. How does a long-term relationship affect communication among economic entities? We study dynamic information design in a repeated “agreement game”, where the state is imperfectly persistent. Information disclosed today influences future beliefs, which results in a novel distortion relative to the static counterpart. We characterize how the optimal mechanism varies with the players’ patience and the state’s persistence. When players are very impatient or very patient, an efficient mechanism is optimal. If their patience is intermediate and the state’s persistence is high, the optimal mechanism may suppress bad news entirely, recommending agreement even when both players would prefer disagreement. If the state’s persistence is also intermediate, the optimal mechanism may do the opposite: recommend disagreement even when both players would prefer agreement, to reduce the informativeness of the bad news conveyed by disagreement.

Title: How Information Systems Practitioners Think in Action: Instantiating Donald A. Schön's General Theory of the ‘Reflective Practitioner’
Authors: Allen S. Lee, Yan Li, Manoj A. Thomas
Affiliations: Virginia Commonwealth University Richmond Virginia USA; Claremont Graduate University Claremont California USA; University of Sydney Sydney New South Wales Australia
Abstract: ABSTRACT To examine how information systems (IS) practitioners think in action, we rely on Donald A. Schön's general theory of the ‘reflective practitioner’—a theory that Schön developed to explain how practitioners in architecture, psychotherapy, engineering, planning, and management think in action, and that we apply to IS practitioners. We go over Schön's explanation that a practitioner's thinking‐in‐action consists of what he calls five moments: knowing‐in‐action, surprise, reflection, criticism and on‐the‐spot experiment. Then, based on our interviews with a technical IS practitioner and a managerial IS practitioner, we show how their thinking in action demonstrates each of the five moments. Finally, based on the five moments, we offer recommendations to IS researchers on how to write papers to better support the work of IS practitioners.

Title: Dynamic Trust Formation in AI ‐Enabled Automation: A Longitudinal Case Study of an Advanced Driver Assistance System
